plants.name: Euphorbia pulcherrima
plants.description: In the wild, poinsettia is a tall, open shrub or small tree that can reach 3–4 metres. Its branch tips carry flaming crimson bracts that look like petals but are really modified leaves. They surround small, clustered yellow-green flowers, so whole hillsides seem lit with red.
plants.location: Mexico and Central America, in seasonally dry forests and hillsides
plants.funFact: The bright red 'petals' are bracts, which are leaves that have changed to attract pollinators. The real flowers are the tiny yellow cups at their center.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: This glossy-leaved evergreen shrub opens delicate, often lightly scented blooms just as most gardens go quiet. Its single or semi-double flowers have silky petals around a boss of golden stamens. They brighten the cool days of late autumn and early winter.
plants.bloomingSeason: Autumn into early winter, typically October or November through December or January
plants.location: Native to Japan; widely grown in temperate gardens of the Northern Hemisphere
plants.funFact: Sasanqua camellias are close relatives of the tea plant, and their seeds are pressed for a cooking and cosmetic oil used in Japan.

plants.name: Ceratopetalum gummiferum
plants.description: This Australian shrub or small tree is covered in tiny creamy flowers in early summer. After the petals fall, the sepals swell and blush from pink to deep red. The effect is a festive, rosy haze across the bush just in time for the holidays.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late spring to early summer, with flowers typically in November–December
plants.location: Eastern Australia, especially the sandstone bushland of New South Wales
plants.funFact: The 'flowers' that turn red are the enlarged sepals, which stay on the plant after the tiny petals drop. That is why Australians bring it indoors as a Christmas decoration, and the red persists until about February.
